pr.title: List the pull requests in a summary's stack in its sidebar
pr.head: 71028a87e875e9f9df15e80be2453f685a85541a

summary: A Projector site serves a review page, called a summary, for each pull request, at reviews/<number>/. A pull request is stacked when its base branch is another open pull request's head branch, so a chain of pull requests builds one change in reviewable layers. Until now, a summary's sidebar named only its own pull request, so a reviewer working through a stack had to go back to GitHub to find the next layer.

This change lists the whole stack in the sidebar: the pull requests beneath this one down to the default branch, and every pull request stacked above any of them. Each row shows the number and title and links to that pull request's summary, or to GitHub when the site has none. The current row is highlighted. A pull request that stands alone keeps its title line, as before.

The stack is worked out when the site deploys, from every summary stored on the summaries ref, so a page learns of a pull request stacked on it later without being republished. The sidebar also drops its head-and-base line, which repeated the page header. The Versions line moves below the sections and becomes a list that starts closed, with one row for each published head and the time it was published, in the reader's time zone.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Summary: the JSON a reviewer writes for one head of a pull request, stored with its diff on the hidden ref refs/projector/summaries.
  • Trunk: the repository's default branch. A pull request based on it is not stacked.
  • bases: the map from each stacked pull request's number to the number of the one beneath it, which stack_bases builds.
  • Stack row: one entry of a page's stack list, with number, title, url, and current.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
The first review, at cd6cd4c81, found that the new unscoped .stack rule in summary.css also styled the “Stacked on #N” note on the Reviews index, which loads summary.css too, and split it across three lines.

The second head, 3710a64b1, reworked the Versions list and left that rule as it was.

This head, 2cccf035d, scopes every stack rule to the sidebar, adds a test that keeps them scoped, shows each stack row's whole title, and takes the review's two suggestions. Its review was clean, with no finding open.

The newest head, 71028a87e, merges main, which had added a repo_root parameter to build_summaries. The merge keeps both parameters, and its review is clean.

groups.title: Working out each page's stack at deploy time
groups.kicker: The site build computes every pull request's stack once and writes it into each page's data.
intro: When the site deploys, build_summaries reads every summary on the ref and writes a page for each head. Before this change it knew nothing about stacks; build_site called stack_bases afterwards, only to mark stacked pull requests on the Reviews index.

Now build_summaries calls stack_bases itself, before writing any page, using each pull request's newest summary. It passes the result to the new stack_rows, which turns it into the rows one page shows, and it returns each entry's stackedOn so the Reviews index reuses the same answer. A base branch that no summary names is still looked up on GitHub at most once per build.
main has since given build_summaries a repo_root parameter of its own, which decides which files the page treats as generated. build_site now passes trunk, lookup, and repo_root by keyword.

checks.text: The new test builds pull request 9 on main, 10 on 9, and both 11 and 12 on 10, and checks that the bottom, the middle, and the top each list [9, 10, 11, 12] with only themselves current. I ran the full suite of 455 tests with Python 3.12, and it passed.

files.note: Moves the stack_bases call into build_summaries and adds stack_rows, which orders one pull request's stack.

checks.text: The pull request map prs takes each number's newest summary, the same one the Reviews index used before, so stackedOn does not change for any entry.

The walk down to the bottom stops at a pull request it has already seen, so two pull requests recorded as each other's base end the loop. I walked that case by hand: the walk from 10 stops at 11, and the walk upward lists 11 and then 10, once each.
pending is used as a stack, so pushing each pull request's branches in reverse order pops the lowest number first, and a branch's own branches follow it before its next sibling.

files.note: One test covers a branched stack, a base with no summary, and a pull request alone; two more check that the stack styles stay scoped to the sidebar and do not cut a title short.

checks.text: This test reads every selector in summary.css that names .stack and requires each to start with .prblock .stack.

groups.title: Drawing the stack in the sidebar
groups.kicker: The summary page renders the stack rows and a closed list of versions, and restyles the sidebar.
intro: The page's renderer is TypeScript in site/src/summary.ts, compiled into site/assets/summary.js, which the repository commits. It reads the page's data.json, whose shape globals.d.ts declares, and now draws the stack rows under the repo#number header.

A row for the current pull request is not a link. A row whose url is empty, a base with no summary on the site, links to the pull request on GitHub. With fewer than two rows the sidebar shows the title line it showed before. A row's title wraps onto as many lines as it needs.

Versions now renders as a details element that starts closed. Each row shows a head's short SHA and, when the head has an at time, when it was published. build_summaries already records that time for every head, from summary_time.

files.note: Declares the optional stack field and the optional at time on each head.
Adds stackList, removes the head-and-base line, and turns headsList into a closed list of versions below the section list.

checks.text: Each title and link is escaped before it reaches the page. npm run check found no type or lint problem.
The times use the reader's locale and time zone, so two readers can see different times for the same head.

files.note: Styles the stack rows and the Versions list in both themes.

checks.text: Every stack rule starts with .prblock, the sidebar block, because the site's home page loads summary.css too and its Reviews table has its own div.stack note. I loaded both stylesheets in headless Chromium, in the home page's order, and the note stayed on one line.

files.note: Compiled from summary.ts; the test suite fails if it differs from a fresh build.
